Write $A/(x+1)+(Bx+D)/(x^2+1)$ [1]. Clearing denominators gives $A+B=8$, $B+D=4$, $A+D=9$ [1]. Thus $A=\frac{13}{2}$, $B=\frac{3}{2}$, $D=\frac{5}{2}$ [1]. Integrate $A/(x+1)$ and $Bx/(x^2+1)$ [1], then $D/(x^2+1)$ and add $C$ [1].

alt.q: Evaluate $\int x^2e^{4x}dx$, showing both uses of integration by parts.
alt.s: Choose $u=x^2$, $dv=e^{4x}dx$ [1]. Then $I=x^2e^{4x}/4-\frac2{4}\int xe^{4x}dx$ [1]. Apply parts to the remaining integral [1] to get $xe^{4x}/4-e^{4x}/16$ [1]. Substitute and simplify [1].

integrals-pdf-board-03.q: Let $I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{16\cos^2x+\sin^2x}$. Evaluate $I$ by substitution, and hence evaluate $J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{x\,dx}{16\cos^2x+\sin^2x}+\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{x\,dx}{16\sin^2x+\cos^2x}$.
integrals-pdf-board-03.s: Put $t=\tan x$ and transform to $I=\int_0^\infty dt/(16+t^2)$ [1]. Its antiderivative is $\frac1{4}\tan^{-1}(t/4)$ [1], so $I=\pi/8$ [1]. Reflect the second integral in $J$; it becomes the first denominator with numerator $\pi/2-x$ [1]. Add the numerators to get $J=(\pi/2)I=\pi^2/16$ [1].

integrals-pdf-board-03.q: Evaluate $\int\sqrt{36-x^2}\,dx$ using $x=6\sin\theta$, and then evaluate the definite integral from $0$ to $6/2$.
integrals-pdf-board-03.s: Choose $-\pi/2<\theta<\pi/2$ so the root is $6\cos\theta$ [1]. The integral becomes $36\int\cos^2\theta d\theta$ [1]. Use $\cos^2\theta=(1+\cos2\theta)/2$ and integrate [1]. Return to $x$ [1]. At the upper endpoint $\theta=\pi/6$; subtract the zero lower-endpoint value to get the stated number [1].

alt.q: Evaluate $\int\frac{x^2}{\sqrt{36-x^2}}dx$ and then evaluate it from $0$ to $6/2$.
alt.s: Set $x=6\sin\theta$ with the usual principal range [1]. The integral is $36\int\sin^2\theta d\theta$ [1]. Apply the half-angle identity and integrate [1]. Return to $x$ [1] and evaluate at $\theta=\pi/6$ and $0$ [1].

integrals-pdf-board-03.q: For continuous $f$ on $[0,6]$, prove the reflection identity for its definite integral. Then evaluate $\int_0^{6}\frac{(x+2)^3}{(x+2)^3+(8-x)^3}dx$. Finally explain why the answer lies strictly between $0$ and $6$.
integrals-pdf-board-03.s: Use $u=6-x$ and $dx=-du$; reverse the transformed limits to establish the identity [2]. For the given integrand reflection interchanges the two cubes [1]. Their fractions add to $1$, so $2I=6$ [1]. Both cubes are positive throughout the interval; the fraction lies strictly between $0$ and $1$, establishing the bound [1].

integrals-pdf-board-03.q: A pump delivers liquid at rate $r(t)=4t+2$ litres per minute for $0\leq t\leq4$. Let $V(t)=\int_0^t r(s)ds$. (i) State $V(0)$. [1] (ii) Find $V\prime(2)$. [1] (iii) Find the volume delivered during minutes 1 to 3. [2] \textbf{OR} Find the average delivery rate over minutes 0 to 4. [2]
integrals-pdf-board-03.s: (i) Equal endpoints give zero [1]. (ii) The fundamental theorem gives $V\prime(2)=r(2)=10$ [1]. (iii) Integrate $r$: $\int_1^3r(t)dt=[2t^2+2t]_1^3$ [1], which equals $20$ litres [1]. OR Average rate is $\frac14\int_0^4r(t)dt$ [1] $=10$ litres/minute [1].

integrals-pdf-board-03.q: A sensor records $s(t)=t-4$ on $0\leq t\leq8$. A signed total is $S=\int_0^{8}s(t)dt$, while total signal magnitude is $M=\int_0^{8}|s(t)|dt$. (i) When does the signal change sign? [1] (ii) Find $S$. [1] (iii) Find $M$, showing the split. [2] \textbf{OR} Find the mean magnitude $M/(8)$. [2]
integrals-pdf-board-03.s: (i) Solve $t-4=0$ [1]. (ii) Symmetry or endpoint evaluation gives $S=0$ [1]. (iii) Split at $4$ [1]; each triangular contribution is $8$, so $M=16$ [1]. OR Compute the same total $M=16$ [1] and divide by $8$ to obtain $2$ [1].

integrals-pdf-board-03.q: A teaching model uses $f(x)=ax+4$ on $[0,2]$. Calibration requires $\int_0^2 f(x)dx=24$. (i) Write the integral in terms of $a$. [1] (ii) Determine $a$. [1] (iii) For $F(x)=\int_0^xf(t)dt$, find $F(1)$ and explain whether $F$ is increasing on $[0,2]$. [2]
integrals-pdf-board-03.s: (i) Integrate $ax+4$ to get $2a+8$ [1]. (ii) Equate to $24$ and solve [1]. (iii) $F(x)=4x^2+4x$, so $F(1)=8$ [1]. Since $F\prime(x)=8x+4>0$ on the interval, it is strictly increasing [1].

integrals-pdf-main-01.s: Integrate $(f-3)^2\geq0$. Expansion gives $\int f^2-2(3)\int f+9\geq0$, hence $\int f^2\geq9$. Nonconstant continuous functions show that equality is not forced.

There are $6$ intervals of width $1/2$ with values $0$ through $5$. Multiplying the integral by $2$ gives $0+1+\cdots+5=15$.
The integral is $a/3+\frac{3}{2}$. Multiply by $6$ to get $2a+9=17$. Therefore $a=4$.

Put $u=\sin x$ and write $\cos^2x=1-u^2$. Then $I=\int_0^1(u^3-u^5)du=1/4-1/6=1/12$. Multiplying by $36$ gives $3$.

integrals-pdf-advanced-01.q: Continuous $f$ satisfies $f(x)+f(2-x)=x^2-2x+6$ for $0\leq x\leq2$. Find $\int_0^2(x-1)^2 f(x)dx$.
integrals-pdf-advanced-01.s: The weight $(x-1)^2$ is unchanged by reflection. Adding the reflected integrals gives $2I=\int_0^2(x-1)^2[(x-1)^2+5]dx$. Set $u=x-1$ to get $2I=2/5+10/3=56/15$, hence $I=28/15$.

integrals-pdf-advanced-01.q: Let $f$ be continuous and strictly positive on $[0,4]$, with $f(4-x)=f(x)$ and $\int_0^4 f(x)dx=3$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-01.s: Reflection gives $\int xf=2\int f=6$, proving A and B. Also $\int(x-2)^2f>0$ because $f>0$ and the square is positive away from $2$. Expansion gives $\int x^2f-4(6)+4(3)>0$, so $\int x^2f>12$. Thus C is false and D true.

integrals-pdf-advanced-01.q: For integers $n\geq0$, let $R_n=\int_0^1x^n/(1+x)dx$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-01.s: A follows by adding the integrands. B follows because $x^{n+1}<x^n$ on $(0,1)$. For C, write $(n+1)R_n-1/2=(n+1)\int_0^1x^n(1-x)/[2(1+x)]dx$. This lies between $0$ and $(n+1)\int_0^1x^n(1-x)dx/2=1/[2(n+2)]$, which tends to zero. D is false since $1/(1+x)<1$ on $(0,1)$.

integrals-pdf-advanced-01.q: Let $F(x)=\int_0^x(t^2-6t+5)dt$ for real $x$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-01.s: $F\prime=(x-1)(x-5)$ has signs $+,-,+$ on the three intervals. This proves A and B and disproves C. Direct integration gives $F=x^3/3-3x^2+5x$, and hence $F(5)=-25/3$.

integrals-pdf-advanced-01.s: The weight $w(x)=x^2-3x+5$ is symmetric about $3/2$. Thus $2I=4\int_0^3w(x)dx=4(9-27/2+15)=42$. Hence $I=21$.
The limit is $\int_0^1x^2/(1+x^3)dx$. Substitute $u=1+x^3$ to get $L=\ln2/3$, so $e^{3L}=2$.

integrals-pdf-advanced-01.s: $A\prime=x^3-2x+4$, $A\prime\prime=3x^2-2$, and $A=x^4/4-x^2+4x$. Hence the four quantities are $4,1,8,8$. The same List II value can legitimately match two entries.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: For $a>0$, define $I(a)=\int_0^1\frac{a}{(a+x)^2}dx$. The equation $I(a)=1/4$ has solution
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: Integrate to get $I(a)=[-a/(a+x)]_0^1=1-a/(a+1)=1/(a+1)$. Thus $a+1=4$ and $a=3$. Positivity ensures there is no pole.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: Let $f$ be continuous on $[0,1]$, with $\int_0^1f=0$ and $\int_0^1xf=1$. The smallest possible value of $\int_0^1f^2$ is
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: $\int_0^1(x-1/2)f=1$. Cauchy--Schwarz gives $1\leq(\int_0^1(x-1/2)^2)(\int f^2)=(1/12)\int f^2$. Equality is attained by $f(x)=12x-6$, which satisfies both conditions. Hence the minimum is 12.

The weight is symmetric under $x\mapsto\pi-x$, so $I=(\pi/2)J$ where $J=\int_0^\pi\sin^2x/(2+\cos^2x)dx$. Write the fraction as $3/(2+\cos^2x)-1$. Substitution $t=\tan x$ on $[0,\pi/2)$ and symmetry give $\int_0^\pi dx/(2+\cos^2x)=\pi/\sqrt6$. Thus $J=\pi(\sqrt{3/2}-1)$, yielding the answer.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: Let $T_n=\int_0^1x^n(1-x)^2dx$ for integers $n\geq0$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: Expansion gives $T_n=1/(n+1)-2/(n+2)+1/(n+3)$, simplifying to A. The ratio in B follows immediately and is less than one, proving C. The formula gives $n^2T_n\to0$, so D is false.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: Let $f$ be continuous on $[-2,2]$ with $f(-x)=f(x)$. Select all statements that must hold.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: A and D follow from oddness and evenness. For B, reflect and add the reciprocal exponential weights, which sum to one: $2I=\int_{-2}^2f=2\int_0^2f$. C fails for $f=1$: pairing $x$ and $-x$ gives $x(1-e^x)/(1+e^x)<0$ for $x>0$, so the integral is negative.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: Let $P(x)=\int_0^x|t-2|dt$ on $\R$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: The integrand is continuous, so $P\prime(x)=|x-2|$ everywhere, proving A. For any $a<b$, the integral of $|t-2|$ over $[a,b]$ is positive, proving strict increase despite the derivative vanishing at one point. The left and right derivatives of $P\prime$ at 2 are $-1$ and $1$, disproving C. Two triangles each of area 2 give D.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: Let $f$ be continuously differentiable and strictly increasing on $[0,2]$, with $f(0)=1$, $f(2)=7$, and $\int_0^2f=6$. Let $g=f^{-1}$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: Parts gives $\int_0^2xf\prime(x)dx=[xf]_0^2-\int_0^2f=14-6=8$. Substitution $y=f(x)$ identifies the inverse integral with the same value, proving A and B and disproving C. Dividing by interval length 6 gives $8/6=4/3$, proving D.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: For $a\in[0,1]$, let $Q(a)=\int_0^1(x-a)^4dx$. Select all true statements.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: Integrating gives $Q(a)=[a^5+(1-a)^5]/5$, proving A. Then $Q\prime=a^4-(1-a)^4$, zero only at $1/2$, and $Q\prime\prime=4a^3+4(1-a)^3>0$, proving B and C. The minimum is $2(1/2)^5/5=1/80$, so D is false.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: \textbf{Common stem for Questions 15 and 16.} Let $A(x)=\int_0^x(t^2-2t)dt$ for $0\leq x\leq3$. Enter the number of distinct zeros of $A$ in $[0,3]$.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: $A(x)=x^3/3-x^2=x^2(x-3)/3$. Its distinct zeros in the interval are $0$ and $3$. The double root at zero is counted once.

\textbf{Common stem for Questions 17 and 18.} For $a\in\R$ define $J(a)=\int_0^2(x^2-a)^2dx$. If $a_0$ is the unique minimizing parameter, enter $3a_0$.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: $J(a)=32/5-16a/3+2a^2$. Hence $J\prime=4a-16/3$, giving $a_0=4/3$. The second derivative is 4, so this is the unique global minimum; $3a_0=4$.

integrals-pdf-advanced-02.q: Using the common stem for Questions 17 and 18, enter $45J(a_0)$.
integrals-pdf-advanced-02.s: Complete the square: $J(a)=2(a-4/3)^2+128/45$. Thus $J(a_0)=128/45$ and multiplying by 45 gives 128.
